多上下文攻击。 攻击跨越监控器只能孤立看到的上下文：通过共享工作区协调的独立会话（多智能体攻击），或单个会话中压缩隐藏了早期攻击步骤（压缩攻击）。
覆盖缺口。 监控器无法干预智能体动作空间的某些部分，或某些信息对其不可见。
策略失效。 提示策略遗漏了有害行为，或监控器未能正确应用策略。

blocks.text: We red-team production blocking monitors (Auto Mode in Claude Code, Guardian in OpenAI’s Codex) with an adversarial agent in an experimental setting with the objective of improving the safety of coding agents. Our most effective attack strategies bypass the monitor using agent-generated prompt injection against the monitor, multi-agent attacks, or malicious compaction. We attempt to improve the robustness of auto-mode by improving tool coverage, transcript formatting and using an agentic monitor stage. We find that robustly preventing multi-context attacks at an acceptable cost remains an open problem.

blocks.text: Blocking monitors (Lindner et al., 2025; Stickland et al., 2025) have been developed and tested for the over-eagerness failure mode. They check each action (e.g. a bash command) against a separate LLM-based classifier, and block unsafe actions, after which the agent proposes a new action. Claude’s Auto Mode and Codex’s Guardian are the most widely used versions of these in production currently. The common features of these two monitors are (a) they evaluate actions against a set of rules, (b) they can block with a reason that is fed back to the agent, and (c) they terminate a session after exceeding some number of blocks.

blocks.text: In this work we study the robustness of blocking monitors against the threat of persistent adversarial agents. We focus on catastrophic harms that can’t be reversed and for which asynchronous monitoring (Lindner et al., 2025) is insufficient. These include exfiltration of data, their own model weights in the most extreme case, and evasion of the blocking monitor by disabling it or creating new unmonitored agents. The four main attack types we study are monitor injection, multi-context attacks, coverage gaps and policy failures.

blocks.text: We study four attack types. By default we use Opus 5 as the attacking model. We also vary the affordances we give to the attacker (see the paper’s appendix), but by default we tell the attacker how the monitor works and give a high level description of the attack.

inlines.text: We study four attack types. By default we use Opus 5 as the attacking model. We also vary the affordances we give to the attacker (see the paper’s appendix), but by default we tell the attacker how the monitor works and give a high level description of the attack.
Monitor injection. Agent-generated content (e.g. code, comments, tool arguments) fools the monitor’s judgement into approving a harmful action.

Multi-context attack. The attack spans contexts the monitor sees only in isolation: separate sessions coordinating via a shared workspace (multi-agent attack), or a single session whose compaction hides earlier attack steps (compaction attack).
Coverage gap. The monitor cannot intervene on parts of the agent’s action space, or certain information is invisible to it.
Policy failure. The prompted policy omits the harmful behaviour, or the monitor fails to apply the policy correctly.

blocks.text: Our architecture for attacker capability evaluations. The attacker agent is tasked with completing a side-task, given a main-task which determines the range of what the monitor should permit. For our arena evaluations we use a Claude Code agent in a Linux sandbox, and for our simulation evals we use an Inspect-based Python agent, and LLM simulated tool call outputs. These contrasting approaches are described below and in the paper’s appendices.

blocks.text: Analytical evaluation looks for discrete vulnerabilities. Reading the monitor’s prompts, code, and integration with the surrounding system directly yields attack hypotheses. Unmonitored tool calls, injection channels, unhandled prompt edge-cases, and points where agent output is promoted to user intent are examples of such vulnerabilities.

blocks.text: Replay-based evaluation scores existing transcripts against a monitor. In a loose analogy with reinforcement learning, replay is off-policy: it is agnostic to the policy that produced a transcript. This makes replay cheap and lets us reuse transcripts from prior work or optimise certain parts of the transcript freely, but it does not capture the attacker vs. defender interaction.

blocks.text: Rollout-based evaluation runs a red-team agent (primarily Opus 5) live against the monitor. We use the agent’s system prompt to steer it toward an attack category and to grant affordances such as knowledge of the monitor formatting. We provide these affordances to understand monitor robustness under worst-case scenarios where the agent is working inside a frontier lab and has access to the monitor’s code. Rollout is the on-policy counterpart to replay: the trajectory is generated by the attacker policy under test as it interacts with the monitor, so rollout success rates are our most credible estimates of real risk.

blocks.text: Monitoring systems have discrete vulnerabilities: some agent tool calls may not be visible to the monitor due to an engineering oversight, and naïve policy wording in the monitor’s prompt can lead to loopholes. We identified and fixed several such vulnerabilities in Claude Code as part of this work.

inlines.text: Monitoring systems have discrete vulnerabilities: some agent tool calls may not be visible to the monitor due to an engineering oversight, and naïve policy wording in the monitor’s prompt can lead to loopholes. blocks.text: The most serious vulnerabilities were unmonitored channels: compaction summaries were not monitored, so an agent could fabricate facts about the environment or the user’s intent and have them treated as trusted context after the compaction. The multi-agent workflow tool was similar: workflow creation and agent-to-agent handoffs let an agent inject instructions into messages that a subsequent agent reads as user authorisation.

blocks.text: The attack is injected into the agent’s Bash command, whose argument spans two lines: the first (red) exfiltrates a credential file, and the second (amber) is forged so that the flattened transcript the monitor reads ends on a harmless looking Bash echo ack. The forged line is not a real command and errors when the shell reaches it, but bash runs the two lines in order, so the exfiltration has already gone through. The monitor mistakenly judges only the final, forged entry and allows the action.

blocks.text: Our strongest mitigation layers two defences:

inlines.text: Our strongest mitigation layers two defences:
Heredoc framing. Each turn is wrapped in a frame <record-h> ... </record-h> whose identifier
is a 48-bit hex string derived from the turn under a per-process key, so it is unguessable to the agent.
Escaping. Within a record we use JSON-L encoding and add an additional layer of escaping.

blocks.text: Injections can be substantially mitigated with heredoc framing and escaping. (a) Prompted attacker in rollout evaluations: in a capability evaluation we show that Auto Mode ++, which combines the JSON-L encoding + additional escaping + heredoc framing, is robust to the attack. (b) Optimisation loop in replay evaluations: the heredoc framing improves robustness against an adaptive attacker.

blocks.text: When each edit is monitored, the specific execute-then-write attack shown above no longer works. Monitoring edits reduces the likelihood the attacker can ever create a malicious script. blocks.text: The monitor evaluates a single context, but agent runs often span many: a session is compacted when its context fills up, and long tasks are often split across agents. An attacker can therefore spread a side-task so that no single context contains a blockable action. We illustrate both attack vectors in the figure above.

blocks.text: Compaction. When an agent’s context window fills up to the model’s context limit, it performs what is called compaction. It generates a summary of the conversation so far and this summary replaces the full history in its context. The agent then continues the task working only from that summary. An attacker can complete a step of the side-task, trigger a compaction, and describe that step in the summary as benign or as work still to be done. Over several compactions the agent writes a script, stages data, and starts processes, each in a context that no longer contains the earlier steps (figure below). We added a check that flags summaries which misstate user intent or recommend harmful next steps. Monitors with this check (auto mode ++ and auto mode strict) catch many more of these attacks than auto mode, but the attack still succeeds at a substantial rate.

blocks.text: Monitoring tool results. Production Auto Mode omits tool results from the transcript it reviews. This keeps the transcript short and reduces the injection attack surface. In a multi-agent attack, however, most of the attack evidence appears only in tool results (e.g. when reading a file written by a previous context), so a monitor that cannot see them cannot see the attack. For this reason including tool results improves recall.

Both this change and the previous one enlarge the injection surface, but we did not observe a higher injection success rate as a result.

blocks.text: Stage ablation. Empirically, the highest recall monitor we test is auto mode strict. This is because we remove stages 1 and 2, which have a higher rate of false negatives. Ablating these stages results in the agentic stage 3 seeing all actions, meaning there is abundant reasoning capacity and context for classifying them. This comes at the cost of much higher latency, so we do not consider strict to be a usable monitor without the fast (albeit less robust) stages 1 and 2. As a result we consider Auto Mode ++ to be the Pareto-optimal monitor.

All monitors block under 1% of the 4,000 benign SWE-chat actions, which we consider acceptable for ordinary coding work. The monitors differ mainly in latency, which depends on how many actions are monitored and how many output tokens each review takes. Auto mode ++ reviews edits inside the working directory and so monitors more actions than auto mode. Strict runs the agent on every action and is too slow for interactive use, so an agentic stage is only viable behind faster stages.

blocks.text: Limitations

inlines.text: Limitations

blocks.text: We assume we can trust the monitor. We treat the monitor as trusted. i.e. we do not study the possibility of the monitor colluding with the attacker (Greenblatt et al., 2023), even though some of our monitor models are close to the attacker in capability and lineage (e.g. for auto-mode ++ we monitor an Opus 5 attacker with an Opus 4.8 monitor). While with current models this proximity is unlikely to result in intentional collusion, such collusion would be more likely with the potentially more coherently misaligned and capable models that may be trained in the future (Carlsmith, 2023; Meinke et al., 2025).

inlines.text: Discussion

blocks.text: We show that production blocking monitors as of September 2026 would not be robust to a persistent, adversarial agent. Against an Opus 5 attacker given a high-level strategy, both Auto Mode and Guardian are bypassed through injection of forged transcript turns, unmonitored edits that change what an already-approved command will run, and attacks spread across compactions and sessions so that no single context contains a blockable action. We typically grant the attacker knowledge of the monitor. Mitigating the threat from adversarial agents is a high priority follow-up to this work.

blocks.text: Most of the vulnerabilities we found have relatively cheap fixes. Framing and escaping the transcript mitigate injection attacks, and monitoring cwd edits prevents execute-then-write attacks.

blocks.text: Our best defences against multi-context attacks are expensive. Defending against them reliably requires the monitor to see and gather context across boundaries, which is in direct tension with cost considerations such as latency. Agentic monitors that probe the transcript and environment perform best against these attacks, but they may be too slow for interactive use unless faster stages are placed in front of them, and those faster stages reduce recall.
